title: How do you use Event Storming to decompose a domain (map commands/triggers → aggregates/state-managers → domain events/outcomes with domain experts), and what are the rules for designing aggregate roots at high TPS — keep aggregates SMALL (a "god" aggregate causes severe optimistic-locking contention), treat the aggregate as the consistency/transaction boundary, and reference OTHER aggregates by ID only (never by direct object reference) so boundaries stay clean and extractable into separate services?
shortTitle: Event Storming and aggregate design at high TPS

s1_definition.profdef: Event Storming is a collaborative workshop technique for exploring a domain by mapping, on a wall of sticky notes with domain experts, the flow of domain events (something that happened, in past tense), the commands that trigger them, and the aggregates that handle those commands and enforce invariants. It surfaces bounded contexts and aggregate boundaries quickly. At high transactions per second, aggregate design follows strict rules: keep aggregates small because a large "god" aggregate becomes a single contended row that serializes writes under optimistic locking; treat the aggregate as the consistency and transaction boundary so one transaction modifies exactly one aggregate; and reference other aggregates by identity only, never by direct object reference, so boundaries stay clean and each aggregate can later be extracted into its own service.
s1_definition.analogy: Event Storming is like gathering the bank's experts around a huge wall and having them stick orange notes for every important thing that happens, such as "Money Transferred" or "Loan Approved", then blue notes for the action that caused it, such as "Transfer Money", then yellow notes for the thing responsible for deciding, such as the Account. By the end the wall shows the whole business as a story, and natural groupings reveal the departments and the small units of control. The high-traffic rule is like saying: do not make one giant master ledger that every clerk must line up to sign, because only one person can hold the pen at a time. Instead give each account its own small passbook so thousands of transfers can happen at once, and when one account needs to know about another, it refers to it by account number, not by physically holding the other passbook.
s1_definition.oneliner: Event Storming maps commands, aggregates, and events with experts to find boundaries; at high TPS keep aggregates small, make the aggregate the transaction boundary, and reference other aggregates by ID only.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Event Storming is a collaborative workshop technique for exploring a domain by mapping, on a wall of sticky notes with domain experts, the flow of domain events (something that happened, in past tense), the commands that trigger them, and the aggregates that handle those commands and enforce invariants. It surfaces bounded contexts and aggregate boundaries quickly. At high transactions per second, aggregate design follows strict rules: keep aggregates small because a large "god" aggregate becomes a single contended row that serializes writes under optimistic locking; treat the aggregate as the consistency and transaction boundary so one transaction modifies exactly one aggregate; and reference other aggregates by identity only, never by direct object reference, so boundaries stay clean and each aggregate can later be extracted into its own service.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Event Storming is like gathering the bank's experts around a huge wall and having them stick orange notes for every important thing that happens, such as "Money Transferred" or "Loan Approved", then blue notes for the action that caused it, such as "Transfer Money", then yellow notes for the thing responsible for deciding, such as the Account. By the end the wall shows the whole business as a story, and natural groupings reveal the departments and the small units of control. The high-traffic rule is like saying: do not make one giant master ledger that every clerk must line up to sign, because only one person can hold the pen at a time. Instead give each account its own small passbook so thousands of transfers can happen at once, and when one account needs to know about another, it refers to it by account number, not by physically holding the other passbook.

**One line to remember:** Event Storming maps commands, aggregates, and events with experts to find boundaries; at high TPS keep aggregates small, make the aggregate the transaction boundary, and reference other aggregates by ID only.

sections.s2_technical:
Event Storming works backwards from events. You gather domain experts and developers and cover a wall with orange sticky notes for domain events, written in past tense, such as `MoneyTransferred`, `PaymentFailed`, `EmiPaid`. Then you add blue notes for the commands that cause them, such as `TransferMoney`, and yellow notes for the aggregates that receive the command, enforce the rules, and emit the event. Arranging these left to right tells the story of the business, and clusters of closely related events reveal bounded contexts, while the thing that owns an invariant reveals an aggregate.

An aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as one unit for data changes, accessed only through its root. The root enforces invariants, for example an `Account` aggregate guarantees the balance never goes negative. The first high-TPS rule is keep aggregates small. If you build a god aggregate, such as a `Bank` aggregate that holds every account, then every transfer must load and lock that one huge object, and under optimistic locking every concurrent write collides on the same version, so writes serialize and throughput collapses. A small `Account` aggregate means two transfers on two different accounts never contend.

The second rule is that the aggregate is the consistency and transaction boundary. One transaction should modify exactly one aggregate and keep its invariants true. Anything that must be strongly consistent lives inside one aggregate; anything that spans aggregates is made eventually consistent through domain events and sagas. For example debiting Rajesh and crediting Priya touches two `Account` aggregates, so it is not one transaction but a saga.

The third rule is reference other aggregates by identity only. Inside the `Transfer` aggregate you store `fromAccountId` and `toAccountId` as strings, never a direct `Account` object reference. This keeps the object graph small, prevents accidentally loading and locking another aggregate, and most importantly keeps the boundary clean so the `Account` aggregate can be extracted into its own service later with no code change to the reference. Optimistic locking with an `@Version` column is how you detect concurrent modification: two writers read version 7, both try to save, one commits version 8 and the other fails and retries. The senior-level nuance is that aggregate size is a direct throughput lever: smaller aggregates mean less contention, more parallelism, and cleaner service extraction, which is why at high TPS you design the smallest aggregate that still protects its invariant.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India processes thousands of transfers per second at peak. Problem 1 — an early design used one giant `Ledger` aggregate holding all accounts, so every transfer locked the same object and under load almost every save failed its version check and retried, crushing throughput. This is exactly why aggregates must be small: a per-account aggregate removes the contention. Problem 2 — a developer put a direct `Account` object reference inside the `Transfer` aggregate, which loaded and locked the counterparty account on every transfer and made it impossible to split accounts into their own service. This is exactly why you reference other aggregates by ID only. Problem 3 — a transfer tried to update both accounts in one transaction and kept deadlocking. This is exactly why the aggregate is the transaction boundary and cross-aggregate work becomes a saga.

The mini-project models a small `Account` aggregate with an optimistic-locking version, a `Transfer` aggregate that references accounts by ID only, and a `TransferSaga` that debits then credits across the two account aggregates. A runnable demo shows two concurrent transfers on different accounts succeeding in parallel, and a version conflict on the same account being detected and retried.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1,000,000) and Priya (CUR3001, 250,000), a transfer of 50,000, then a concurrent 10,000 debit on Rajesh.

Step 1: Event Storming produced the model: the command `TransferMoney` is handled by a saga across two small `Account` aggregates, emitting the event `MoneyTransferred`. The `Transfer` aggregate holds only account IDs, not objects.

Step 2: The saga executes. It debits the `SAV2001` aggregate, which modifies only that aggregate and bumps its version to 1. Because the aggregate is small, this write contends with nothing else on other accounts.

Step 3: The saga credits the `CUR3001` aggregate, modifying only that aggregate and bumping its version to 1. The transfer is marked COMPLETED. Two aggregates changed, but as two separate steps, not one cross-aggregate transaction.

Step 4: Now a concurrency scenario. Reader A takes a snapshot of Rajesh's version. Writer B debits Rajesh 10,000 first, bumping the version. When reader A tries to commit against its stale version, the optimistic-lock check detects the mismatch.

Step 5: The conflict is caught and the operation retries with the fresh version. This is how small aggregates plus optimistic locking give high throughput: unrelated accounts never block each other, and only genuine same-account races retry.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 INFO === Small aggregates: transfer across two accounts (saga) ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 INFO Transfer COMPLETED SAV2001 → CUR3001
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 INFO Rajesh=950000 v1, Priya=300000 v1
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 INFO === Optimistic lock conflict on the SAME account ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 SEVERE Version conflict on SAV2001 expected 1 but was 2
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:20 WARNING Retrying with fresh version 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Event Storming wall (left → right story):
  [TransferMoney cmd] → (Account aggregate) → [MoneyTransferred event]

  Runtime transfer (SAGA across SMALL aggregates):
    Transfer{from="SAV2001", to="CUR3001", amt=50000}   ← IDs only, no objects
      │
      ▼
    TransferSaga.execute()
      │ step 1: Account(SAV2001).debit(50000)  → balance 950,000, version 1
      │           (locks ONLY this small aggregate)
      │ step 2: Account(CUR3001).credit(50000) → balance 300,000, version 1
      │           (locks ONLY this small aggregate)
      ▼
    Transfer.status = COMPLETED

  Concurrency on SAME aggregate:
    Reader A snapshot v1 ──┐
    Writer B debit → v2 ───┤→ assertVersion(1) ✗ conflict → retry with v2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Event Storming is a collaborative workshop where I put domain experts and developers in front of a big wall and map the business as a story. We start with orange sticky notes for domain events written in the past tense, such as Money Transferred or EMI Paid, then add blue notes for the commands that cause them, like Transfer Money, and yellow notes for the aggregates that handle the command and enforce the rules. Arranging them left to right reveals the flow of the business, clusters of related events reveal bounded contexts, and the thing that owns an invariant reveals an aggregate. It is the fastest way I know to get experts and engineers to agree on boundaries.

When it comes to designing aggregates for high transactions per second, I follow three strict rules. The first is to keep aggregates small. At National Bank of India, an early design used one giant Ledger aggregate holding every account, so every transfer loaded and locked the same object, and under optimistic locking almost every write collided on the same version and had to retry, which collapsed throughput. A small per-account aggregate fixes this because two transfers on two different accounts never contend.

The second rule is that the aggregate is the consistency and transaction boundary. One transaction modifies exactly one aggregate and keeps its invariant true, such as the balance never going negative. Anything that spans aggregates, like debiting Rajesh and crediting Priya, is not one transaction but a saga with eventual consistency driven by domain events. The third rule is to reference other aggregates by identity only. Inside the Transfer aggregate I store the from and to account IDs as strings, never a direct Account object, which keeps the object graph small, prevents accidentally locking the counterparty, and keeps the boundary clean enough that the Account aggregate can later be extracted into its own service with no change to the reference.

The thread tying it together is that aggregate size is a direct throughput lever. Smaller aggregates mean less lock contention, more parallelism, and cleaner service extraction, while a god aggregate becomes a single hot row that serializes every write. So at high TPS I always design the smallest aggregate that still protects its invariant, use an optimistic-locking version column to detect genuine same-aggregate races, and push everything cross-aggregate onto sagas and events.
